commandWords.means: State what happens or what is observed, in sequence, without giving reasons.
commandWords.doThis: Give observations in the order they occur, e.g. colour changes, gas produced, using correct chemical names.

commandWords.means: Give reasons using chemical ideas such as bonding, particles or energy.
commandWords.doThis: State the effect, then say why using a chemistry principle, e.g. 'because ions are free to move and carry charge'.

commandWords.means: Use a pattern, trend or data to suggest what would happen in a new but related situation.
commandWords.doThis: Refer to the trend or rule (e.g. reactivity series, periodic table trend) and apply it directly to the new example.

commandWords.means: Adjust numbers in front of formulae so atoms of each element are equal on both sides.
commandWords.doThis: Count atoms of each element on both sides, add whole-number multipliers until they match; never change a formula's subscripts.

commandWords.means: Weigh up advantages and disadvantages of a method, process or data set to reach a judgement.
commandWords.doThis: Give points for and against with reference to the given data, then state and justify an overall conclusion.

commandWords.means: Apply chemical knowledge to an unfamiliar context; more than one answer may be accepted.
commandWords.doThis: Use a chemistry principle you know (bonding, reactivity, rates) and apply it logically to the new example given.

commandWords.means: Work out a numerical answer using given data and a formula.
commandWords.doThis: Write the formula used, substitute values with units, show each working step, and state the final answer with units.

commandWords.means: State similarities and differences between two substances, methods or sets of data.
commandWords.doThis: Write sentences that directly contrast both items, e.g. using 'whereas' or 'both', not two separate descriptions.

commandWords.means: Support a choice or statement using evidence or a chemical principle.
commandWords.doThis: State the choice, then give the specific data point or rule that supports it.

commandWords.means: Work out an answer by combining given information logically rather than by direct recall.
commandWords.doThis: State the pieces of given information used and the chemical rule that links them to reach the conclusion.

commandWords.means: Name a specific substance, ion, or feature from given data or a test result.
commandWords.doThis: Give the specific chemical name or formula, not a general description.

items.detail: React an acid with an insoluble base/metal until excess remains, filter, then evaporate and crystallise. Measured: mass of crystals formed. Controlled: same acid concentration and volume. Examiners want the reason for using excess solid (to ensure all acid reacts) and slow evaporation (larger, purer crystals).

Use a burette to add acid to a known volume of alkali with indicator until the end point (colour change) is reached. Measured: titre volume (cm3). Controlled: concentration and volume of the alkali, same indicator. Examiners want a rough titration first, then concordant results (within 0.10 cm3) for the mean.

Pass current through an aqueous solution using inert (graphite/platinum) electrodes and identify products at each electrode. Measured: gas/product formed and any colour or mass change. Controlled: same current, same concentration and volume of solution.

Mix reactants (e.g. acid and alkali, or acid and metal) in an insulated cup, record temperature at intervals. Measured: temperature change. Controlled: volume/concentration of reactants, use of a lid and insulation to reduce heat loss.

React reactants (e.g. sodium thiosulfate and acid, or marble chips and acid) and measure gas volume with a gas syringe over time, or time until a cross disappears (turbidity). Measured: volume of gas vs time, or time to reach a fixed cloudiness. Independent variable: usually concentration, temperature or surface area, kept the others constant.

Spot samples on chromatography paper above a solvent, allow solvent to rise, measure distances to calculate Rf values. Measured: distance moved by spot and by solvent front. Controlled: same solvent, same paper, baseline drawn in pencil.

items.term: RP7: Identifying ions (flame tests and chemical tests)
items.detail: Use flame tests for metal ions, and add reagents (NaOH, dilute acid, silver nitrate, barium chloride) to identify cations and anions from colour changes/precipitates. Measured: flame colour or precipitate colour observed. Controlled: clean nichrome wire between tests to avoid contamination.

Test water samples for pH and dissolved solids, then distil a sample and compare boiling point/purity of the distillate to the original. Measured: volume of distillate, temperature during distillation, mass of residue. Controlled: same volume of sample, same heating rate.

sections.title: Reactivity series and displacement rules
sections.note: Order from most to least reactive.

items.detail: Potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, (carbon), zinc, iron, (hydrogen), copper, silver, gold. Carbon and hydrogen are included as reference points though not metals.
A metal above hydrogen in the series reacts with dilute acid to produce a salt plus hydrogen gas; metals below hydrogen (copper, silver, gold) do not react with dilute acids.
Potassium, sodium, lithium and calcium react with cold water to form a metal hydroxide plus hydrogen gas; magnesium reacts very slowly with cold water but reacts with steam.
A more reactive metal will displace a less reactive metal from a solution of its salt or from its oxide, e.g. Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu.
Metals below carbon in the reactivity series (e.g. iron, zinc, copper) can be extracted from their oxide by reduction with carbon, because carbon displaces them.
Metals above carbon in the reactivity series (e.g. aluminium, potassium, sodium) must be extracted by electrolysis because carbon cannot displace them.
In displacement, the more reactive metal is oxidised (loses electrons) and the less reactive metal ion is reduced (gains electrons).
Reactivity increases going down Group 1 because the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more easily lost.
Reactivity decreases going down Group 7 (halogens) because it becomes harder to gain an extra electron as atomic radius increases.
A more reactive halogen will displace a less reactive halide from solution, e.g. chlorine displaces bromide: Cl2 + 2KBr -> 2KCl + Br2.

moles = mass (g) / relative formula mass (Mr). Use to convert a measured mass into an amount for reacting-mass calculations.
mass (g) = moles x Mr. Use to predict the mass of product or reactant needed.
concentration (g/dm3) = mass of solute (g) / volume of solution (dm3). Use for making up solutions of known strength.
concentration (mol/dm3) = moles of solute / volume of solution (dm3). Use for titration and reacting-volume calculations.
divide cm3 by 1000 to get dm3. Always convert before using concentration in mol/dm3.

moles = concentration (mol/dm3) x volume (dm3). Find moles of the known solution first, use the balanced equation mole ratio to find moles of the unknown, then convert to concentration or mass as needed.

percentage yield = (actual mass of product / theoretical maximum mass of product) x 100. Always less than 100 percent due to incomplete reactions, losses during transfer/filtration, or side reactions.
atom economy = (Mr of desired product / sum of Mr of all reactants) x 100. High atom economy means less waste and is important for sustainable industrial processes.
1 mole of any gas occupies 24 dm3 (24,000 cm3) at room temperature and pressure (20 degC, 1 atm).
moles = volume of gas (dm3) / 24. Use for gas volume calculations at RTP, e.g. finding gas produced in a reaction.
Convert all reactant masses to moles, divide each by its balancing number in the equation; the smallest result identifies the limiting reactant.
Sum of the relative atomic masses of all atoms shown in the formula, e.g. Mr of CaCO3 = 40 + 12 + (16x3) = 100.
In a closed system, total mass of reactants = total mass of products; an apparent mass change in an open system usually means a gas has entered or escaped.
CnH2n+2. Saturated hydrocarbons (single C-C bonds only). First four: methane CH4, ethane C2H6, propane C3H8, butane C4H10.
Complete combustion: alkane + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water. Incomplete combustion (limited oxygen) produces carbon monoxide and/or soot (carbon) instead.
CnH2n. Unsaturated hydrocarbons containing at least one C=C double bond. First three: ethene C2H4, propene C3H6, butene C4H8.
Shaken with orange bromine water: alkenes decolourise it to colourless via addition across the double bond; alkanes do not change its colour.
Addition reactions add atoms across the C=C bond, e.g. with hydrogen (forms an alkane), water (forms an alcohol), or a halogen (forms a dihalogenoalkane).
CnH2n+1OH, functional group -OH. First four: methanol, ethanol, propanol, butanol.
React with sodium to release hydrogen gas; burn in air (combustion) to give CO2 and water; can be oxidised (e.g. by microbial action or oxidising agents) to carboxylic acids.
Ethanol is made by fermentation of sugar with yeast at 25-35 degC in anaerobic conditions, or industrially by hydration of ethene with a catalyst.
CnH2n+1COOH, functional group -COOH. First four: methanoic, ethanoic, propanoic, butanoic acid.
Weak acids - only partially ionise in water, so react less vigorously than strong acids of the same concentration; react with carbonates to give a salt, water and carbon dioxide.
Carboxylic acid + alcohol -> ester + water, using an acid catalyst (e.g. concentrated sulfuric acid). Esters have distinctive sweet smells and the functional group -COO-.
Formed when many unsaturated alkene monomers join together, opening their double bonds, with no other product formed, e.g. many ethene -> poly(ethene).
Formed when monomers with two functional groups join, releasing a small molecule (usually water) at each new bond, e.g. formation of polyesters.

sections.title: Atmosphere and using resources fact bank

items.detail: Formed from intense volcanic activity releasing mostly carbon dioxide and water vapour, with little or no oxygen, similar to the atmospheres of Mars and Venus today.
As the Earth cooled, water vapour condensed to form the oceans.
Carbon dioxide was locked up in sedimentary rocks and fossil fuels, and was dissolved into the oceans, then absorbed by algae and plants for photosynthesis.
Algae and plants evolved and produced oxygen by photosynthesis over billions of years, gradually building up the roughly 21 percent level in today's atmosphere.
About 80 percent nitrogen, about 20 percent oxygen, with small amounts of carbon dioxide, water vapour and noble gases.
Carbon dioxide, methane and water vapour absorb infrared radiation reflected from Earth's surface and re-radiate it, keeping the planet warmer than it would otherwise be.
Burning fossil fuels increases carbon dioxide; agriculture (livestock, rice paddies, landfill) increases methane.
Rising sea levels, more extreme weather, changing rainfall patterns, and changes in the distribution of species.
The total amount of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases released over the full life cycle of a product, service or event.
Using more renewable/low-carbon energy, carbon capture and storage, using less energy, and international agreements to cut emissions.
Carbon monoxide (toxic, from incomplete combustion), sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides (cause acid rain and respiratory problems), particulates (soot, cause global dimming and health problems).
Finite resources (e.g. crude oil, metal ores) are used faster than they form and will run out; renewable resources (e.g. timber, biofuel crops) are replenished at a comparable rate to their use.
Extracting and processing raw materials; manufacturing and packaging; use and operation; disposal at end of life - transport is included at every stage.
Choose an appropriate source, filter through wire mesh then sand beds to remove solids, then sterilise with chlorine, ozone or ultraviolet light.
Distillation (evaporate then condense) or reverse osmosis (force water through a membrane); both require large amounts of energy, making them expensive.

1 hour 45 minutes, 100 marks. Covers atomic structure, bonding, quantitative chemistry, chemical changes, energy changes. Aim for roughly 1 minute per mark; do titration/mole calculations last if short on time since they take longer per mark.

1 hour 45 minutes, 100 marks. Covers rate and extent of change, organic chemistry, chemical analysis, the atmosphere, using resources. Aim for roughly 1 minute per mark; attempt all required-practical based questions even if unsure, as method marks are available.
Skim all questions, identify calculation-heavy questions (titration, moles, percentage yield) and plan to allocate them enough time rather than rushing at the end.
Check every calculation answer has the correct unit, every formula has balanced charges/atoms, and no multiple-choice question is left blank.
Read all options before choosing, cross out options you know are wrong, and never leave a multiple choice question blank - a guess has a chance of being right.
Underline the command word (describe, explain, evaluate, calculate) in each question before writing, to avoid describing when an explanation is required or vice versa.

items.term: Using the mark allocation as a guide
items.detail: A question worth 3 marks needs roughly 3 distinct linked points; a 1-mark question needs a single short, precise answer - do not overwrite short-answer questions.
Always show the formula used and every substitution step, even if unsure of the final answer, since method marks are awarded for correct working.

topics.name: C4 Chemical Changes Part 2: Electrolysis
subtopics: Electrolytes, electrodes, anode and cathode, and why ions must be free to move
Electrolysis of molten ionic compounds: metal at the cathode, non-metal at the anode
Electrolysis of aqueous solutions and the rules for which product forms
Cathode rule: hydrogen forms unless the metal is less reactive than hydrogen
Anode rule: oxygen forms unless a halide ion is present, in which case the halogen forms
Writing half equations at each electrode and balancing electrons
Extraction of aluminium from bauxite, and why cryolite is added
Why electrolysis is used for metals more reactive than carbon
Required practical: electrolysis of aqueous solutions using inert electrodes
Oxidation is loss, reduction is gain of electrons (OILRIG)
The reactivity series, displacement reactions and reduction of metal oxides by carbon

cards.front: What forms at the cathode during electrolysis of molten lead bromide?
cards.back: Lead metal, because positive metal ions are attracted to the negative cathode and are reduced.

cards.front: State the cathode rule for electrolysis of aqueous solutions.
cards.back: Hydrogen is produced unless the metal present is less reactive than hydrogen, in which case the metal is deposited.

cards.front: State the anode rule for electrolysis of aqueous solutions.
cards.back: Oxygen is produced unless a halide ion is present, in which case the halogen is produced.

cards.front: Write the half equation for hydrogen forming at the cathode.
cards.back: 2H+ plus 2e- gives H2.

cards.front: Write the half equation for oxygen forming at the anode from hydroxide ions.
cards.back: 4OH- gives O2 plus 2H2O plus 4e-.

cards.front: Why is cryolite added during aluminium extraction?
cards.back: It lowers the melting point of aluminium oxide, reducing the energy and cost required to keep it molten.

cards.front: Why can aluminium not be extracted by reduction with carbon?
cards.back: Aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot displace it from its oxide - electrolysis is required.

cards.front: What does OILRIG stand for?
cards.back: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain - of electrons.

cards.front: Why must an ionic compound be molten or dissolved for electrolysis?
cards.back: The ions must be free to move to the electrodes to carry the charge.

cloze: During electrolysis, positive ions move to the {{c1::cathode}} and are {{c2::reduced}}.
{{c1::Cryolite}} is added to aluminium oxide to lower its {{c2::melting point}}.
Metals more reactive than {{c1::carbon}} must be extracted by electrolysis.
The half equation at the cathode for hydrogen is 2H+ + 2e- gives {{c1::H2}}.

cards.front: What is the general formula of the alkanes?
cards.back: CnH2n+2.

cards.front: What is the general formula of the alkenes?
cards.back: CnH2n.

cards.front: Name the first four alkanes.
cards.back: Methane, ethane, propane, butane.

cards.front: How does fractional distillation separate crude oil?
cards.back: Oil is heated and vaporised, then fed into a column that is hot at the bottom and cool at the top; each fraction condenses where the temperature matches its boiling point range.

cards.front: How does bromine water distinguish an alkane from an alkene?
cards.back: Alkenes decolourise orange bromine water to colourless by addition across the double bond; alkanes leave it orange.

cards.front: Why is cracking carried out?
cards.back: Long-chain fractions are in low demand, so they are broken into shorter, more useful alkanes and into alkenes needed to make polymers.

cards.front: Give the conditions for catalytic cracking.
cards.back: Heat the long-chain hydrocarbon to vaporise it and pass the vapour over a hot catalyst.

cards.front: What is the functional group of a carboxylic acid?
cards.back: COOH.

cards.front: What are the products when an alcohol reacts with a carboxylic acid?
cards.back: An ester and water, using an acid catalyst.

cards.front: Give the conditions needed for fermentation.
cards.back: Aqueous sugar solution, yeast, warm temperature around 25 to 35 degrees Celsius, and anaerobic conditions.

cards.front: How does addition polymerisation differ from condensation polymerisation?
cards.back: Addition polymerisation joins alkene monomers with no other product; condensation polymerisation joins monomers with two functional groups and loses a small molecule, usually water, each time.

cards.front: What are proteins made from?
cards.back: Amino acid monomers joined by condensation polymerisation into polypeptides.

cards.front: How do boiling point and viscosity change as hydrocarbon chains get longer?
cards.back: Both increase, while flammability decreases.

cloze: The functional group of an alkene is the {{c1::carbon-carbon double bond}}.
Alkenes turn bromine water from {{c1::orange}} to {{c2::colourless}}.
The general formula of the alkanes is {{c1::CnH2n+2}}.
Fermentation requires sugar, {{c1::yeast}}, warmth and {{c2::anaerobic}} conditions.
An {{c1::ester}} is made from an alcohol and a carboxylic acid with an acid catalyst.

cards.front: How is Rf value calculated?
cards.back: Distance moved by the substance divided by the distance moved by the solvent front.

cards.front: What is a formulation?
cards.back: A mixture that has been designed as a useful product, with each component present in a measured quantity, e.g. paint, alloy or medicine.

cards.front: How do you test for carbon dioxide?
cards.back: Bubble the gas through limewater; it turns milky or cloudy.

cards.front: How do you test for chlorine gas?
cards.back: Damp litmus paper is bleached white.

cards.front: State the flame test colours for lithium, sodium, potassium, calcium and copper.
cards.back: Lithium crimson, sodium yellow, potassium lilac, calcium orange-red, copper green.

cards.front: What colour precipitate does iron(III) form with sodium hydroxide?
cards.back: Brown.

cards.front: What colour precipitate does iron(II) form with sodium hydroxide?
cards.back: Green.

cards.front: How do you test for a sulfate ion?
cards.back: Add dilute hydrochloric acid then barium chloride solution; a white precipitate forms.

cards.front: How do you test for a halide ion?
cards.back: Add dilute nitric acid then silver nitrate solution: chloride gives white, bromide cream, iodide yellow precipitate.

cards.front: Give three advantages of instrumental methods of analysis.
cards.back: They are more accurate, more sensitive and faster than chemical tests, and can work on very small samples.

cards.front: Why must the chromatography baseline be drawn in pencil?
cards.back: Pencil graphite is insoluble in the solvent, so it will not travel up the paper and interfere with the results.

cards.front: How does melting point indicate purity?
cards.back: A pure substance melts at one specific temperature; a mixture melts over a range of temperatures.

cards.front: What are the four stages of a life cycle assessment?
cards.back: Extracting and processing raw materials, manufacturing and packaging, use and operation during lifetime, and disposal at end of life including transport at every stage.

cards.front: What is potable water?
cards.back: Water that is safe to drink - it has low levels of dissolved salts and microbes, but is not chemically pure.

cards.front: Describe UK treatment of fresh water to make it potable.
cards.back: Pass through filter beds of wire mesh and sand to remove solids, then sterilise with chlorine, ozone or ultraviolet light.

cards.front: Why is desalination expensive?
cards.back: Distillation or reverse osmosis both require large amounts of energy.

cards.front: How is sewage sludge treated and what useful products result?
cards.back: By anaerobic digestion, which produces methane biogas as a fuel and digested waste that can be used as fertiliser.

cards.front: What two substances are needed for iron to rust?
cards.back: Water and oxygen.

cards.front: How does sacrificial protection work?
cards.back: A more reactive metal such as zinc or magnesium is attached to the iron; it corrodes in preference, protecting the iron.

cards.front: Describe phytomining.
cards.back: Plants absorb metal compounds from low-grade ore; the plants are burned and the ash, which contains a high concentration of the metal compound, is processed to extract the metal.

cards.front: Describe bioleaching.
cards.back: Bacteria are used to produce leachate solutions containing metal compounds, from which the metal can be extracted by displacement or electrolysis.

cards.front: Why do thermosetting polymers not melt?
cards.back: Strong covalent cross-links between the polymer chains hold them rigidly in place.

cards.front: What is a composite material?
cards.back: A material made of two components: a reinforcement of fibres or fragments held in place by a matrix or binder.

cards.front: How is borosilicate glass different from soda-lime glass?
cards.back: It is made from sand and boron trioxide and melts at a higher temperature, so it is more resistant to thermal shock.

cloze: {{c1::Potable}} water is safe to drink but is not chemically {{c2::pure}}.
Rusting requires both {{c1::water}} and {{c2::oxygen}}.
In {{c1::sacrificial}} protection, a more reactive metal corrodes instead of the iron.
{{c1::Thermosetting}} polymers contain covalent {{c2::cross-links}} and do not melt.
{{c1::Phytomining}} uses plants to absorb metal compounds from low-grade ores.

topics.name: C6/C10 The Haber Process and NPK Fertilisers
subtopics: Raw materials: nitrogen from air, hydrogen from natural gas
Conditions: 450 degrees Celsius, 200 atmospheres, iron catalyst
The reversible reaction N2 + 3H2 in equilibrium with 2NH3 and the forward reaction being exothermic
Le Chateliers principle applied to temperature and pressure changes
Why 450 degrees Celsius is a compromise between yield and rate
Why very high pressure is limited by cost and safety
Recycling unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen
NPK fertilisers and the three essential elements
Making ammonium nitrate, ammonium sulfate and phosphate fertilisers
Comparing industrial and laboratory preparation of ammonium sulfate

cards.front: State the conditions used in the Haber process.
cards.back: 450 degrees Celsius, 200 atmospheres pressure, and an iron catalyst.

cards.front: Where do the raw materials for the Haber process come from?
cards.back: Nitrogen from the air and hydrogen from natural gas.

cards.front: Why is 450 degrees Celsius used rather than a lower temperature?
cards.back: The forward reaction is exothermic so a lower temperature would give a higher equilibrium yield, but the rate would be too slow - 450 degrees is a compromise.

cards.front: Why does high pressure increase the yield of ammonia?
cards.back: There are 4 moles of gas on the left and 2 on the right, so increasing pressure shifts the equilibrium to the side with fewer molecules, favouring ammonia.

cards.front: What do the letters NPK stand for in fertilisers?
cards.back: Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.

cards.front: How is ammonium sulfate made industrially versus in the lab?
cards.back: Industrially in several integrated stages on a large continuous scale; in the lab by a single-batch titration of ammonia solution with dilute sulfuric acid followed by crystallisation.

cards.front: State Le Chateliers principle.
cards.back: If a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change, the position of equilibrium shifts to counteract that change.

cards.front: How do you calculate the number of moles from a mass?
cards.back: Moles equals mass in grams divided by relative formula mass.

cards.front: What is Avogadros constant?
cards.back: 6.02 times 10 to the power of 23 - the number of particles in one mole of a substance.

cards.front: How do you calculate percentage yield?
cards.back: Mass of product actually made divided by the maximum theoretical mass, multiplied by 100.

cards.front: How do you calculate atom economy?
cards.back: Relative formula mass of the desired product divided by the total relative formula mass of all reactants, multiplied by 100.

cards.front: What volume does one mole of any gas occupy at room temperature and pressure?
cards.back: 24 cubic decimetres.

cards.front: Explain why increasing temperature increases the rate of reaction.
cards.back: Particles have more kinetic energy so they collide more frequently, and a greater proportion of collisions have energy above the activation energy.

cards.front: How does a catalyst increase the rate of reaction?
cards.back: It provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, without being used up.

cards.front: What is a limiting reactant?
cards.back: The reactant that is completely used up first and therefore limits the amount of product formed.

cards.front: How do you find the rate of reaction at a specific time from a graph?
cards.back: Draw a tangent to the curve at that time and calculate its gradient.

cards.front: Give three reasons why percentage yield is less than 100 percent.
cards.back: The reaction may be reversible, some product may be lost in handling or separation, and side reactions may produce other products.
